A Christmas Carol was written by Charles Dickens and first published in 1843. It is perhaps the most beloved story ever written about the season of goodwill, and it has never been out of print. Dickens wrote it to remind people to be generous and kind to those in need. The tale of Scrooge's change of heart has warmed readers for well over a hundred and fifty years.

Ebenezer Scrooge was the meanest, coldest, most miserly man in all the city. He loved money above everything and cared for no one. He kept his office freezing to save on coal, paid his poor clerk a pittance, and had no kindness in him at all. When people wished him a happy season of goodwill, he only scowled and grumbled that it was all nonsense.

image.note: A grim, pinched old man hunched over money at a cold desk; a shivering clerk nearby; cheerless, icy

pages.text: On a cold winter's eve, Scrooge's cheerful nephew came to invite him to a warm family dinner. Scrooge sent him crossly away. Two kind men came collecting for the poor, and Scrooge refused them a single coin. His overworked clerk, Bob Cratchit, timidly asked for the next day off to spend with his family, and Scrooge grudgingly, grumpily allowed it. Then he went home alone to his dark, empty house.

image.note: Scrooge coldly turning away his cheerful nephew and two charity collectors; his poor clerk cowed; hard-hearted

pages.text: That night, alone in his gloomy house, Scrooge had a terrible fright. The ghost of his dead business partner, Jacob Marley, appeared before him, wrapped in heavy chains. Marley had been as greedy and cold as Scrooge in life, and now, he moaned, he was doomed to wander in misery, weighed down by the chains he had forged through his own selfishness.

image.note: The ghost of Marley, bound in heavy chains and cash-boxes, moaning before a terrified Scrooge; supernatural, warning

pages.text: Marley had come with a warning, and a last chance. Scrooge, he said, was heading for the very same dreadful fate, unless he changed his ways. That very night, three spirits would visit him: the ghosts of Christmases past, present and yet to come. Then Marley vanished into the dark, leaving Scrooge trembling and afraid in his cold bed.

image.note: Marley's ghost fading away, one chained arm raised in warning; Scrooge cowering; the promise of three spirits

pages.text: The first spirit came at the stroke of one: the Ghost of Christmas Past, a gentle, glowing figure. It took Scrooge by the hand and carried him back through the years, to scenes of his own boyhood. Scrooge saw himself as a lonely schoolboy, and then as a hopeful young man who had once been warm, and merry, and in love, before greed had slowly hardened his heart.

image.note: A glowing gentle spirit showing Scrooge scenes of his own youth; a lonely boy, a hopeful young man; memory, longing

pages.text: Watching his younger, kinder self, Scrooge felt an ache he had not felt in years. He saw the moment he had chosen money over love and let the warmth die out of him. Tears sprang to his old eyes. For the first time in a very long time, the cold miser was beginning to feel something soften and stir within his frozen heart.

image.note: Old Scrooge weeping quietly as he watches his younger self make a cold choice; the first thaw; moving

pages.text: The second spirit was the Ghost of Christmas Present, a huge, jolly giant crowned with holly, surrounded by a feast. It showed Scrooge how others were spending the season with warmth and love, even those with very little. Above all, it took him to the humble home of his own poor clerk, Bob Cratchit, to see how that family kept the day.

image.note: A jolly holly-crowned giant spirit; a warm, modest family gathering glimpsed through a window; joy amid poverty

pages.text: In that small, poor house, Scrooge saw the Cratchit family full of love despite their hardship. And he saw their youngest child, Tiny Tim, a sweet and gentle boy who was very ill and walked with a little crutch. The spirit warned that unless things changed, the frail child would not live to see another year. Scrooge, to his own surprise, found his heart breaking for the little boy.

image.note: A frail, sweet child, Tiny Tim, on a small crutch at a humble family table; Scrooge watching, deeply moved; tender

pages.text: The final spirit was the most frightening: the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come, a silent, hooded figure that pointed the way with a shadowy hand. It showed Scrooge a bleak future. A man had died, unloved and unmissed, and people spoke of him coldly, caring only for what they might take from his empty house. No one mourned him at all.

image.note: A tall, silent, hooded spirit pointing; a bleak scene of a death mourned by no one; ominous, chilling but not gory

pages.text: With dawning horror, Scrooge was shown the neglected grave of that unloved man, and read upon the cold stone his own name. This was his future, if he did not change. And in the poor Cratchit home, he saw a small empty chair and a little crutch, carefully kept, where Tiny Tim used to sit. Scrooge fell to his knees, weeping, and begged for the chance to change his ways.

image.note: Scrooge on his knees before a gravestone bearing his own name; then a small empty chair; grief and desperate hope

pages.text: Scrooge awoke in his own bed on Christmas morning, and found he was still alive, and that there was still time. Overjoyed, a changed man, he threw open his window to the bright, snowy day. He had never felt so light and happy. The cold, greedy old miser was gone forever, and a warm, generous, laughing man stood in his place.

image.note: Scrooge throwing open his window on a snowy morning, arms wide, laughing with pure joy; utterly transformed; radiant

pages.text: And Scrooge kept his promise gloriously. He sent the largest turkey in the shop to the Cratchit family. He raised Bob's wages and became a second father to little Tiny Tim, who did not die, but grew well and strong. He gave generously to the poor, made peace with his nephew, and became known as a man who knew how to keep the season of goodwill better than anyone alive.

image.note: A joyful Scrooge bringing gifts and warmth to the Cratchit home; Tiny Tim well and happy; generosity, warmth

pages.text: So the man who had begun as the coldest heart in the city ended as one of the kindest. His story shows that it is never too late to change, that greed only chains the soul, and that true happiness is not found in hoarding riches but in giving, in kindness, and in love. And Tiny Tim, who saw the good in everyone, said it best of all: "God bless us, every one."

image.note: A warm final scene of Scrooge feasting happily with the Cratchits and his nephew; love and light; closing, joyful
